It was fun to revisit this game a decade later after I originally played it at release, it still totally holds up. The game still has one of my all-time favorite framing devices for a game, with the whole conceit being the experience is a 1970s sci-fi B-movie with director's commentary running over it. It's equal parts silly, funny, and charming.

Gameplay-wise, it is a totally serviceable beat 'em up, but the game is absolutely elevated by the visual style and commentary track. The creature designs (strings and all!) do a great job of looking like low budget practical effects & costumes, and the stop motion animation on them is top-notch. 

The overall level design is novel as well, with it truly being one giant vertical tower that you are progressing up throughout the experience. The game encourages you to fling yourself off and explore to find a lot of the hidden collectibles and fun Easter eggs; you can instantly teleport back to solid ground with the press of a button, and there's a ton of checkpoints that you can fast travel between as well.

Definitely one of my favs in the ACE Team catalog; it's a super unique experience that doesn't outstay its welcome.

From what I know, few people have tried to incorporate third-party narration as an integral part of their game. What I mean is, a third-party entity in the game looking over your progression and providing commentary based on what you do. A whole lot of these games are either visual novels or walking simulators, like The Stanley Parable or Slay the Princess. But we do also have some games that incorporate this idea with an action gameplay, like ICEY or Bastion.
The Deadly Tower of Monsters belongs to the second group. It makes use of narrators that provide commentary from the very beginning of the game to the very end of it, and uses a brilliant reasoning for its inclusion. But the quality of the overall package is not satisfactory.

[h2]Do people even know what a DVD menu is nowadays?[/h2]
Admittedly, The Deadly Tower of Monsters has a very interesting, and dare I say unique, story premise. It presents the experience as the live watching of a B-Movie from the 50s that is going to be getting the VHS to DVD treatment, and an audio engineer has been assigned to record the director's comments on the movie to be included on the disc as special content. Therefore, nearly everything you do in the game is accompanied/narrated by the director and the sound engineer partaking in discussions.
I have to say, the game starts extremely well in this regard and fully leans into the B-Movie looks and feels. It perfectly showcases the techniques and effects used in the B-Movies of that era through its audio and visuals (such as corny dialogues, usage of stop motion animation and puppets, usage of home appliances as gadgets for futuristic movies, off-screen errors being mistakenly visible in the final product, etc.) accompanied by the director talking about them, ranting about the current movie industry and mentioning how the process of shooting his movie went on.
I also really appreciate the addition of extra lines of dialogue to take nearly every situation into account. Simply waiting in one place for prolonged periods of time, dying to an enemy or doing something wrong can result in different reactions from the director. For example, you will get different lines of dialogue if you either decide to land on a haystack in the beginning of the game or deliberately miss it. However, the narration does not stay charming throughout the whole game.
As you get closer to the end, the humor just wears off and the director starts to show that he is actually very abusive towards his crew instead of his initial clueless and/or dumb impressions. Not only that, he is absent from the final chapter of the game, leaving the audio engineer to state his thoughts on the movie and provide the humor which is frankly some of the worst in the game. All of this then culminates in a 4th wall breaking ending that made absolutely no sense to me and left me disappointed with how random it was. These story and narration issues have had catastrophic effects on the whole game, as The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a game that carries its gameplay through the narration, not the opposite or both in tandem.

[h2]I shouldn't get bored in a 4 hour game, yet here we are...[/h2]
Unfortunately, The Deadly Tower of Monsters does not have what it takes to keep the players interested for the whole experience when it comes to the gameplay. It stays like a regular top-down action platformer from the beginning to the end, with nothing getting introduced to break the stale flow of the game. Now this might seem like nonsense as the game can be beaten in about 4 hours but trust me, it gets boring very fast.
A part of this boredom comes from how the gameplay is designed. On one hand, we have platforming challenges that are really nothing special, whenever they are not infuriating (we'll get to this soon). On the other hand, combat is not satisfying either. You get all these weapons and defensive abilities, and see a variety of enemies, just to find out that most of them are useless and barely change the flow of combat. You collect plenty of gold from enemies and boxes, just to find out the gears are far more important, and the skill system is based on what achievements you have unlocked in a playthrough instead of other things, so most of what you have collected will be useless. You get all these interesting-looking bosses, but the fights against them are lackluster and not fun at all. And whatever else that the game offers is not enough to make you more invested in it.
The whole gameplay mechanic of shooting enemies that approach from below is interesting at first, yet gets overused later on and honestly adds nothing to the experience. Switching characters to get past various obstacles or having some enemies being resistant to certain weapon types is a good idea, yet the backtracking needed to change them is tedious in so many cases, as character/weapon changers are not always present next to a checkpoint. Locking collectables behind obstacles that require a later-acquired ability is a reoccurring thing in games, yet it's not really beneficial to do here (unless you are going for 100%) because of both the aforementioned backtracking and also the new weapons not always being better and worth the investment.

[h2]Can you just hold that straight?[/h2]
Then we have the issue of the camera system. Earlier in the game, the camera view seems to be fine and manageable; But as you progress further in the game, the camera angles will get worse. They constantly get placed in awkward angles, negatively impacting depth perception and making proper platforming a hell to go through, like the flying saucers before chapter 4. It can also move or zip around in a very fast and very uncomfortable manner (like the Emperor's Throne section where it just violently moves around, or if you try to jump off from the tower) if you dare go somewhere other than where the game expects you to.
And all of this is such a shame, as I really like the presentation here. When I revisited the game with more experience under my belt, I was shocked at how well the first hour of the game went on. I loved the audiovisual presentation and even laughed at some of the jokes as they hit too close to home for me. But the further I progressed, the less I was inclined to finish the game. If it wasn't for the fact that I was in the final parts of the penultimate chapter of the game, I would have never tried to bring myself to finish it.


[h2]TL;DR[/h2]
Starts great with an interesting concept, but cannot keep the momentum going till the end as humor, combat and platforming get progressively more boring as the game goes on, despite the low playtime.

I absolutely loved the humour and attention to detail in this game, which is why I'm very sad that I didn't end up enjoying it as a whole. Although this game does some things very well, there were just too many things that it doesn't.

As I mentioned, the story in this game is the highlight. This game sets itself up as a commentary track on an old, low budget movie, and it works surprisingly well. The narration is usually funny, and the various references and world/enemy design are really creative as well, with some enemies moving like they were filmed in stop motion, or flying enemies having obvious wires that are keeping them suspended. Unfortunately, it wasn't all good, as the fourth and final chapter of the game really missed the mark for me. The story suddenly changed and got really weird, and it lost a lot of the magic for me. That was really unfortunate, as I was loving it until that point, but it resulted in a fairly disappointing ending.

The gameplay is alright, although I didn't find it to be anything spectacular. The platforming is decent, but the combat leaves a lot to be desired, and usually boils down to spamming your favourite weapons until the enemy stops moving. Upgrades weren't very exciting either, as character upgrades were hard to get (as they're locked behind achievements) and weapon upgrades felt a bit pointless once you'd upgraded your favourite ones. There's three characters that you can play as, which have some different abilities (and are occasionally required to progress), but my friend and I played as Scarlet for most of the game, as she moves faster than the other two. This felt like a bit of an odd design decision, and made the game feel like a slog whenever it forced us to play as someone else (especially the robot, as it moves significantly slower).

All of this would probably have been forgivable if it weren't for the very poor implementation of local co-op. I understand that the game very clearly states that it wasn't designed for multiplayer when you start the game, but I wasn't expecting it to be barely playable, especially when it's advertised on the store page as co-op. I played through the entire game with a friend using Steam Play Together, and issues we encountered included:
[list]
[*] The camera only follows the first player, so the second player constantly got lost off screen.
[*] The second player gets the ability to teleport to the first player, but this sometimes wouldn't work or would happen unexpectedly.
[*] The second player can't pan the camera down, and it's extremely jarring for the second player when the first player does this unexpectedly.
[*] When aiming down, the second player doesn't get any reticle, making it almost impossible to aim.
[*] The second player can't interact with any of the terminals for upgrading or changing weapons or characters.
[*] Although money is shared between both players, the second player doesn't get any weapon upgrades the first player purchases and is stuck with the base version of all weapons.
[*] The health and ammo is shared between both players, so combat is often harder as a result.
[*] Many critical objects like elevators and lifts would behave bizarrely or wouldn't activate at all for the second player
[/list]
These issues left us pretty frustrating, especially since the store page doesn't mention that this game doesn't work well in multiplayer, and just advertises that the game is co-op.

Although the game looked nice, and the world and enemy design was good, the game was fairly unstable. On top of the issues with multiplayer that were already mentioned, we encountered numerous other bugs, like getting hit by enemies through walls, certain sound effects being extremely loud, terminals becoming impossible to interact with, lifts getting stuck or characters clipping through them, flickering textures, characters randomly being launched away at high speeds, and the entire screen going black.

[b]TL;DR[/b] Although this platformer has a really unique premise, and the narration and level design is pretty interesting and enjoyable, the final portion of the story was very disappointing, the combat felt somewhat uninteresting, the multiplayer was barely playable, and the game was very unstable. This game might be worth it in singleplayer if you get it on sale, but I otherwise can't recommend it.

The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a hilarious send-up to the Sci-Fi B-movies of classic Hollywood, with an appropriately all-encompassing retro vibe. The whole thing plays like you're in a DVD remaster of an old sci-fi classic complete with funny 'DVD commentary' by the director and producer that lasts through the entire game, while you're playing. As one of three heroic protagonists you'll ascend an evil emperor's tower, blasting and slashing away at hordes of monsters, aliens, violent apes, and colossal bosses. The whole thing can be completed in just a few hours, but the game is so charming and enjoyable you'll likely want to play through it again right away. Unlock all those weapon upgrades you might have missed, collect those Steam achievements/cards or play using one of the other video filters (or lack of one)

In short, it's unique, doesn't overstay its welcome, and offers some truly funny dialog and great looking enemies. If you like humor and old monster movies, this is your game!

[h1]Reseña de \The Deadly Tower of Monsters\[/h1]

[h2]Resumen[/h2]
¿Listos para cortocircuitar vuestros sesos con explosiones de rayos láser y saltos entre antenas espeluznantes? \The Deadly Tower of Monsters\ es ese bonito homenaje a los filmes B de ciencia ficción que jamás pedimos, pero que, oh sorpresa, resultó ser bastante entretenido. Pues sí, amigos, es hora de escalar la infame torre, luchar contra monstruosidades que podrían haber sido sacadas de un liquidador de disfraces y, por supuesto, salvar el día como buenos clichés ambulantes.

[h2]Aspectos importantes e interesantes[/h2]
- **Narrativa**: Se presenta como un DVD de una vieja película comentado por el director envejecido. Eso es oro puro, chicos.
- **Estilo visual**: Es como ver tus juguetes de infancia cobrar vida y patear traseros alienígenas en technicolor.
- **Jugabilidad**: Saltar, disparar y esquivar, no necesitas un doctorado para manejar este juego, lo cual agradecemos profundamente.

[h2]Aspectos por mejorar[/h2]
- **Repetitividad**: Subir la torre puede volverse tan repetitivo como las excusas de mi perro cuando se come mis deberes.
- **IA de los enemigos**: A veces parece que te enfrentas a unos muy dedicados conos de tráfico. No es que me queje de golpear cosas que no se mueven, pero un poco más de chispa no haría daño.

Aunque es una expresión que no me gusta, The Deadly Tower of Monsters es una carta de amor al cine syfy de los 50-60, sobre todo a la peli Planeta Prohibido, cuya portada homenajea la de este videojuego. Unexpectedly good! Nostalgic for 80s and 90s kids. You've never played a game like this! As you run through the 3rd person full 3D world, the narrator constantly makes jokes about the scene and what you are doing.

Climb the tower and the camera angle automatically changes to guide you on what the game wants you to do next. It's mostly linear but fun. I did get stuck once but reloading from the auto-save points was reliable.

First 20 min wasn't really my gaming style but it kept surprising me with it's humour and sprinkling of new "game mechanics" from start to the very end. I was impressed how well it handled incorporating so many references to other games sprinkled around including Mario, Space Invaders, Frogger, Donkey Kong, Dr Who, Mars Attacks, just a few simple platformer timed jumps, and more! Any other game would feel disjoint having so many styles of game play but this really does it well with short bursts. Addictive like a poker machine because you never know what's next.

The game designers are masterminds! Well paced and balanced for casual gamers. It's not difficult but you can also die very quickly with some enemies until you figure out how to kill them.

Mostly no loading time and jumping off the tower is encouraged to rack up new achievements which gives you Level Up skill points. The tower is cleverly designed to make you explore and jumping off at different places gives you access to new locations.

The ending is perfect! Well worth slogging though :)

PROS
* Fun story with great narration
* Dying is forgiving and instant respawn from most places
* Fun variety of melee and ranged weapons with levelling up
* 3D world is seamless and you can jump from the very top level to the bottom
* Its much bigger than you first imagine
* Achievements are actually quite fun to do and not arbitrary

CONS
* Simple battle mechanics. Extra mechanics exist but aren't necessary to master eg "parry" which is a dodge attack, dodge roll, deflect using a sword, jump attack (like Mario), jump + smash.
* Must do achievements to level up / get skill points
* Can get stuck in just a few places
* Weapons mostly do the same damage, no resistance / vulnerability
* Money is arbitrary and not really needed, you'll always have enough to level up
* Map wasn't really useful for me
* Cant zoom out camera, may feel restrictive

Já faz um bom tempo que a mídia gamer especializada e os gamers adoram se referir à ERA DOURADA DOS GAMES como o período compreendido entre 1986 a 1994, mais precisamente a era dos consoles ATARI, NES, SNES, MASTER SYSTEM, SEGA GENESIS e NEOGEO. TDToM é uma bela aventura cinematográfica recheada de gráficos belíssimos que exploram o charme dos filmes antigos e entregam, por vezes, cenas belíssimas de se ver com inimigos e chefes enormes na tela causando espanto e surpresa.

I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

The Deadly Tower of Monsters is a quirky twin-stick shooter/top-down beat 'em up with a premise of being a DVD commentary of a cheap 50's sci-fi movie that was made in the 70's.  And the game hangs a lot of its charm on the player finding that premise endearing.

Because the gameplay is without a doubt rough-around-the-edges.  As a top-down/isometric game with a mostly fixed camera that tracks and curves around the terrain, much of it being a circular deadly tower, movement and aiming can feel a disorienting.  Though, the aiming feels like it has enough of a lock-on mechanic to not require precise control.  It does leave the melee and range fighting feel a little stiff and flat though.  

Where The Deadly Tower of Monsters adds a interesting mechanic is with its 'aim below' gameplay.  Every now and again, the player will receive a warning that enemies are approaching from below followed by space invader-like icons to where these enemies approximately are to whatever ledge or surface.  The player can then activate 'aim below' where the game becomes something like an upside-down rail shooter.  The trouble is that much of the ledge the player is standing on fills the screen, many times its a curved ledge and enemies wander in and out of the screen.  The whole thing is equally, if not, more disorienting than regular gameplay.  Doubly so, because unless the player is ready and knows where these sections are, it can same critical seconds to find the ledge to initiate this game mode with enough time to access enemies and stat blasting.  Occasionally, I found it was just easier to let the enemies reach the platform I was on and battle them in the regular mode.  Which seems like a shame, as this 'aim down' mode seemed like a decent idea to break up the gameplay.

Throughout The Deadly Tower of Monsters, the player will pick up additional ranged and melee weapons.  All of which can be upgraded at stations provided the player has enough of the resources (3 different cogs and gold) to do so. Their effects are noticeable, but just barely and the visual or audio changes are more notable than the actual power-ups.  And getting the resources via the secrets can be a tad daunting.  Largely due to the camera.  Which makes looking around or find the path to aim or get to the secret tricky.

The visuals, music and sound are pretty good.  The game really likes to play up the whole movie scene angle.  With various film imperfections like film scratches, black and white, fingerprints on the lens, etcs.  The director commentary really sells the idea.  And it's this commentary that I think makes or breaks the the game.  I personally found the director commentary quite amusing and would pause to listen to it or go out of my way to hear more of it.  However, I equally could see it getting on the nerves of some gamers.  Ultimately, without it, there isn't much to The Deadly Tower of Monsters.

The Deadly Tower of Monsters recommendation largely hinges on whether the player is a fan of old movies, DVD commentaries and/or MST3K.  The twin-stick shooter/brawler mechanics are serviceable but mediocre.  The way the camera moves can be disorientating at best and nauseating at worst.  The puzzles seem more about where to look and/or stand than much of anything else.  The 'aim down' mode feels unpolished.  Not to say the game is bad.  It just doesn't have any gameplay that stands out.  I like The Deadly Tower of Monsters, but I know its the DVD commentary of a bad sci-fi film doing all of the heavy lifting with a game that is just okay.

If you don't have a good time, you won't necessarily have a bad time. You could just have an okay time. And that's good too.
